source: Laban et al. (2023) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in The FlipFlop Experiment
finding: Challenging a model with a short follow-up makes it flip answers. Every model flips more often when its first answer was wrong than when it was right, yet it still flips many right answers, so accuracy always falls.
numbers: 10 LLMs, 7 classification tasks, 5 challenger utterances, 67,640 runs. Headline: 46% flipped, 17% mean accuracy drop (per-model table averages about 44% and 16%). Correct-to-flip vs wrong-to-flip: GPT-4 10.4% vs 30.3%; GPT-3.5 54.9% vs 79.7%; Claude V1.3 59.9% vs 71.4%; Claude V2 53.4% vs 69.7%; Gemini-Pro 40.9% vs 52.1%; PaLM-bison 9.7% vs 12.5%; Llama2-7b 65.5% vs 77.7%.
limits: Older models (2023). Classification tasks with fixed labels. Headline and table averages differ slightly, unexplained.
agent_relevance: Gives the flip rate on right vs wrong answers asked for in gap 4. Flip rate on right answers is the cost a stance-holding guardrail must remove; flipping on wrong answers is the part worth keeping.

source: Laban et al. (2023) FlipFlop, fine-tuning mitigation (Table 4)
finding: Fine-tuning Mistral-7b on non-sycophantic dialogues cut the accuracy loss about 60% without hurting first-turn accuracy. Sycophancy was reduced, not removed.
numbers: Base FlipFlop effect -9.5% average, -26.5% on hardest unseen subset; best variant -3.8% and -12.9%. Initial accuracy 59.5% vs 60.8% base. Apologies 60% to 1.4%. Flip rates of tuned models not reported.
limits: One small model, training not prompting. No right-vs-wrong flip split after tuning, so stubbornness on wrong answers is not measured.
agent_relevance: Shows stance-holding can be added without a first-answer accuracy cost, but only by training. Our scaffold must test a code-level version and report the flip split.

source: Li, Krishnan, Padman (2026) Consistency of Large Reasoning Models Under Multi-Turn Attacks
finding: Nine reasoning models were attacked with eight follow-up types over eight rounds after a correct first answer. Eight of nine beat the GPT-4o baseline on position-weighted consistency; Claude 4.5 did not and lost accuracy under attack.
numbers: MT-Consistency set, 4-option factual MCQ, 39 subjects. Initial accuracy 82.29% to 94.86% vs GPT-4o 78.14%. Average accuracy over rounds: GPT-5.1 98.92%, GPT-OSS 98.53%, Grok-4.1 97.06%, DeepSeek-R1 89.91%, Claude-4.5 86.31%, GPT-4o 91.29%. Welch d vs baseline 0.12 (R1) to 0.40 (Grok-4.1); Claude-4.5 d=-0.27, p<0.001. No-flip trajectories: GPT-OSS 591, Grok-3 558, GPT-5.1 545, Claude 4.5 317.
limits: Trajectory table layout partly garbled in the extracted text; use headline figures only. Conditions on questions the model first answered correctly, so it measures only the cost side (loss of right answers). Factual MCQ only.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 for 2025-26 models: reasoning helps but is model-specific. Pressure attacks differ by model, so a stance guardrail must be tested per model.

source: Li et al. (2026) Multi-turn attacks: failure taxonomy and confidence defence
finding: Self-doubt and social conformity cause half of failures. Confidence-aware generation, which helps standard LLMs, fails on reasoning models because long traces make them overconfident.
numbers: Five failure modes: self-doubt, social conformity, suggestion hijacking, emotional susceptibility, reasoning fatigue; first two = 50% of failures. Random confidence embedding beat targeted extraction. Misleading suggestions worked on all nine models. Expert-appeal attack had the lowest flip rates; consensus appeal hit Claude 4.5 hardest; closed 'Are you sure?' gave near-zero flips in GPT-OSS, moderate in R1.
limits: Abstract plus results text read; per-attack numbers are in figures not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports G10: do not gate stance on the model's stated confidence. Hold stance by code check (G2, G3), not by self-reported certainty.

source: Hong et al. (2025) Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues (SYCON-Bench)
finding: Across 17 LLMs, alignment tuning raised sycophancy; scale and reasoning optimisation lowered it. Reasoning models still fail when they argue the logic instead of addressing the user's belief.
numbers: Metrics Turn of Flip (higher better, max 5) and Number of Flip. Debate ToF with plain prompt: o3-mini 4.95, GPT-4o 4.90, DeepSeek-r1 3.91, DeepSeek-v3 3.27, Qwen2.5-7B 1.10. Within a family larger models cut sycophancy up to 81.4%, reasoning variants up to 21.6%. Base vs instruct stance retention at turn 2 (Table 3): one pair 71.43 vs 14.52.
limits: Free-form multi-turn, LLM-judged stance. Open-weight and API models of 2025.
agent_relevance: Third-person and anti-sycophancy prompts are the cheap prompt-level stance guardrail to test.

source: Hong et al. (2025) SYCON-Bench prompt mitigations (Table 4)
finding: A third-person 'Andrew' persona raised Turn of Flip a lot in debate; adding an explicit anti-sycophancy instruction helped most on unethical queries. Gains were absent on false-presupposition items.
numbers: Debate ToF, You prompt vs Andrew prompt: Qwen2.5-7B 1.10 to 4.02; Llama-3.1-8B 2.81 to 4.56; Gemma-2-9b 2.36 to 3.87; DeepSeek-v3 3.27 to 4.40; DeepSeek-r1 3.91 to 4.83. Unethical ToF You vs Andrew+Non-sycophantic: DeepSeek-r1 3.21 to 4.59; GPT-4o 1.49 to 2.82; Claude-3.7 2.69 to 3.95. False presupposition ToF stays 1.4 to 3.4 for all prompts (DeepSeek-r1 3.30 vs 3.32). Paper claim: up to 63.8% (debate) and 28% (unethical).
limits: Higher ToF means slower flipping, but the benchmark does not check the model is right to hold, so stubbornness on wrong stances is not measured. Persona is one of four prompts.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a prompt cue helps hold stance on opinion and ethics items but does not fix false-presupposition items, which need a premise check, not a stance cue.

source: Tie et al. (2025) Can LLMs Correct Themselves? A Benchmark of Self-Correction (CorrectBench)
finding: Across 11 correction methods, intrinsic correction helps on hard tasks, hurts on several easy ones, and adds little on strong reasoning-trained models while costing time. A plain CoT baseline stays competitive.
numbers: Tasks: HotpotQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA, GSM8K, AQuA, MATH, HumanEval. GPT-3.5 Self-Refine: HotpotQA -14.21, CS-QA -12.25, GSM8K -5.14, MATH +7.74, GPQA +10.88. Reflexion-v1 negative on nearly every cell, e.g. GPT-3.5 CS-QA -24.53, GSM8K -22.64. Self-Refine GPQA gains +21 to +27 on several larger models.
limits: Appendix table layout garbled in text extraction, row-to-model mapping uncertain for some rows; only clearly labelled rows cited. Not certainty-gated.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 1: in 2025 intrinsic correction is still task-dependent and often negative. Gain appears where base accuracy is low (GPQA), loss where it is high. Supports certainty or difficulty gating (G1, G12).

source: Tie et al. (2025) CorrectBench, reasoning LLMs section (RQ3)
finding: Authors conclude reasoning models already embed correction, so added methods give marginal gains and extra cost.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3 base is top-2 or top-1 on all seven datasets (GSM8K 95.12, MATH 85.02, GPQA 31.35); mixing methods raises accuracy but lowers efficiency.
quote: reasoning LLMs ... already embed sophisticated error-detection and correction processes
limits: DeepSeek-V3 is a general model distilled from R1, not R1 itself; the explanation is the authors', not tested by ablation.
agent_relevance: Prompted critique on top of a reasoning model is probably wasted; keep critique for non-reasoning drafters or low-certainty items. No certainty-gated re-run of Huang exists in what we found, so gap 1 is only partly closed.

source: Silver et al. (2025) Language Models can perform Single-Utterance Self-Correction of Perturbed Reasoning
finding: When wrong steps are injected into a model's own chain of thought, open-weight models often fix them within the same response, even models not tuned for long CoT.
numbers: Abstract only read: robust correction across a range of open-weight models and math datasets; no numbers on the page.
limits: Injected errors, not natural errors; no rates read. Differs from Huang (2023) because correction happens inside one generation, not a prompted second pass.
agent_relevance: A single-pass check-as-you-go is different from a prompted critique round, in line with G1 (doubt on signal, not a scheduled pass).

source: Does Thinking More always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models (2025)
finding: Adding 'Wait' style rethinking first raises then lowers accuracy; parallel independent paths with a vote beat extended thinking in the same budget.
numbers: Up to 20% higher accuracy for parallel thinking vs extended thinking at equal budget (abstract).
limits: Abstract only; benchmarks and models not read.
agent_relevance: Backs G11 and G9: more serial doubt is not free; spend on parallel attempts.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning (full text)
finding: Critic models are scored on erroneous and correct solutions separately, so false alarms can be read off. Strong critics keep false alarms low (correct-sample accuracy 90 to 98%); weak ones either miss errors or flag nearly everything.
limits: Math only; open models use 8-sample majority vote. The critic is given a numbered step list, a stronger setting than free self-critique. No token cost reported per critique.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: false-alarm rate on correct solutions is 100 minus correct accuracy: o1-mini 2.1% (GSM8K) and 4.9% (MATH); GPT-4o 8.8% and 23.4%. A critic operator must be measured on correct items before use; small models give near-total false alarms or near-total misses.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: PRM vs critic generalisation
finding: Process reward models trained on easy data do not generalise to harder sets and lose to prompted critics; best open critic QwQ-32B-Preview is near GPT-4o but behind o1-mini.
numbers: Skywork-PRM-7B F1 GSM8K 70.8, MATH 53.6 (threshold from GSM8K); Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K 68.2 and 62.6. Reasoning-trained critics beat all PRMs on average.
agent_relevance: Locating the failing step is a capability that scales with reasoning training; code-located failures (G2) avoid depending on it.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis (ERIC abstract record)
finding: Verified from the abstract record. 341 effect sizes from quasi- or true-experiments with standardised CT measures. Dialogue, authentic problems and mentoring helped most.
numbers: Random-effects mean g+ = 0.30 (p<0.001), heterogeneous (p<0.001); k=341 effect sizes. Effective strategies exist for generic and content-specific CT.
quote: Critical thinking (CT) is purposeful, self-regulatory judgment.
limits: Abstract read, not the full text, so moderator effect sizes (dialogue, authentic, mentoring) are not read. Measures are mostly short standardised tests.
agent_relevance: Closes the g+ part of gap 6. Mean effect is small; background only for the agent.

source: Huber and Kuncel (2016) Does College Teach Critical Thinking? A Meta-Analysis (ERIC abstract record)
finding: Abstract confirms substantial gains in CT skills and dispositions over a normal college experience, and no steady extra gain from curriculum-wide CT programs. The abstract contains no numbers.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. The earlier note of about 0.59 SD and 50th to 72nd percentile is NOT confirmed.
limits: Full text not obtained (publisher gave 403, OpenAlex gave 429).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays half open: keep the percentile figure unconfirmed. Human-side background only.

source: Audit of this schema against the six Delphi skills (SCHEMA.md v0.2)
finding: Mapping of the six Facione skills to schema parts. Interpretation = S1 (restate, input hygiene). Analysis = S2 and O3. Evaluation = S4, S7, S8, G3. Inference = S3 and S5. Explanation = only the one-line 'what is wrong' in S5 and the lesson line in S9. Self-regulation = G1, G6, G7, G12 and the S6 impasse detector.
numbers: Skills with a code-checked gate: evaluation, self-regulation, inference (3 of 6). Skills resting on a model-written line only: explanation. Interpretation has S1 but no check that the restatement matches the task.
limits: Own reading of the schema, not an experiment; the mapping is a judgement.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 answer: weakest are explanation (no output a checker can use) and an interpretation-fidelity check. Candidate test: restatement fidelity at S1 with and without a back-translation check.

source: Audit of Delphi dispositions against guardrails (SCHEMA.md v0.2)
finding: Dispositions with a code-level analogue: suspend judgment = G1 and G6; seek evidence = G3 and G8; open-mindedness to alternatives = S7 counterexample test and O1 to O8 at impasse. Holding a position under social pressure has none (no stance guardrail).
numbers: 4 of 5 grouped dispositions (inquisitiveness, open-mindedness, evidence-seeking, suspend-judgment, fair-mindedness) have a schema analogue; resisting pressure has none (see d01 to d06).
limits: Own mapping; no measured disposition scores.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: dispositions can be measured separately as behaviours: flip rate under challenge (d01, d03), false-alarm rate on correct items (d11), answer revision on a fresh disconfirming input (S7). No prompt-only 'be open-minded' manipulation with measured effect was found.

source: Gap status: transfer of a general CT prompt across domains for LLMs (McPeck question)
finding: No direct test found. Nearest evidence is CorrectBench: the same intrinsic method helps GPQA and MATH, hurts HotpotQA and CS-QA, so a general critique procedure does not transfer evenly; effect depends on task and base accuracy.
numbers: Same method, GPT-3.5 Self-Refine: GPQA +10.88, MATH +7.74, HotpotQA -14.21, CS-QA -12.25.
limits: Indirect; not a designed test of domain-general vs domain-primed prompts. No paper found within the search budget.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Evidence leans toward McPeck's side for prompted self-critique: effect is task-specific.

source: Gap status: Ennis-Weir as blinded multi-run probe (no new source)
finding: No new source opened. No study with 10+ runs and a fixed judge was found.
limits: Not opened this session; relies on the earlier correction note.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open; plan: 10+ runs per arm, fixed judge that sees no arm label (G5).
